oil.summary: Crude markets are sending mixed signals today. WTI slipped just 0.55% to $102.22/bbl while Brent dropped a sharper 3.84% to $110.91, widening the spread amid volatile geopolitical flows. The most consequential late-session headline: Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed following a naval mine strike that set an oil tanker ablaze — a development that will demand close attention overnight. Europe announced a release of 42 million barrels from emergency reserves, half diesel, in a direct policy response to the $11 billion/month import cost surge tied to the Iran war. On the supply diplomacy front, the US temporarily eased Russia sanctions and Washington is reportedly discussing post-war Sakhalin joint ventures and Druzhba pipeline deals. UBS data shows Russian exports only 10% below pre-war levels. Products sold off hard — heating oil -5.0%, RBOB -2.82% — while Sinopec posted Q3 profit up 64% and Carlos Slim liquidated $1.15 billion in US oil equities.
drivers: Iran declares Strait of Hormuz closed after tanker mine strike — acute supply disruption risk to ~20% of global oil flows
Europe releasing 42 million barrels of emergency stocks to cap retail fuel prices ahead of winter
US-Russia sanctions easing and post-war energy mega-deal talks add competing downside pressure on medium-term prices

gas.summary: Natural gas markets diverged sharply across regions today. Henry Hub gained 4.69% to $2.95/MMBtu, extending a solid weekly gain of 5.47%, likely reflecting winter demand positioning. European TTF fell 3.19% to €97.51/MWh on the day but remains up 34.76% on the month — a stark reminder of the structural supply squeeze. The month's gains are underpinned by the Iran war disruption and ongoing Russian supply uncertainty. On the supply side, Equinor doubled its resource estimate for the Afrodite North Sea discovery. Trafigura signed a $1.5 billion, five-year deal to supply over 150 TWh of gas to Germany's SEFE, signalling long-term European import dependency. Shell nearly doubled Q3 profits to $10.8 billion on record LNG margins. A sanctions-violation allegation against Polar LNG's Alaska project adds regulatory risk to US LNG supply growth.
drivers: Henry Hub up 4.69% on the day; TTF up 34.76% month-on-month, both reflecting winter demand and war-driven European supply anxiety
Trafigura-SEFE 150 TWh supply deal and Equinor's doubled Afrodite estimate highlight Europe's scramble to secure non-Russian gas
Polar LNG faces Russian-financing allegations, adding sanctions risk to a key prospective US LNG export project

power.summary: News flow in the power and carbon sector is relatively thin today. EU carbon allowances (EUA) edged up 0.22% to $84.97/EUA, maintaining a steady monthly uptrend of nearly 5%, broadly consistent with elevated gas prices keeping carbon costs supported in the power stack. TTF's sharp monthly rise of 34.76% continues to feed through to generation costs. UK National Grid announced up to $532 million investment to extend the IFA France-UK interconnector through 2050, a significant infrastructure commitment for cross-border power security. The US is actively promoting American nuclear technology across Central Asia and the Caucasus. A CCS project by Heidelberg Materials in Edmonton reportedly cleared all technical tests but failed on investment economics — a cautionary signal for the carbon capture pipeline. Ukraine's 1,000-drone strike hitting a St. Petersburg oil terminal is a reminder that energy infrastructure attacks remain a live risk.
drivers: EUAs holding firm near $85 with monthly gains intact, underpinned by elevated TTF and winter demand expectations
UK National Grid's $532M IFA interconnector extension to 2050 reinforces long-term cross-border power security investment
Heidelberg Materials CCS project failure on investment test highlights persistent financing gap for industrial carbon capture
